title: Claude Safety and Trust Boundaries
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to define trust boundaries around Claude and decide where independent validation, authorization, or human review is required. After completing it, learners can distinguish a model response from permission to perform an action.
objectives: Identify where untrusted data crosses a boundary in an application that uses Claude.
Distinguish model-generated recommendations from authorization to perform consequential actions.
Choose independent validation or human review appropriate to the consequence of an action.
Explain why model-level safeguards do not replace application-level controls.

sections.title: Source update
paragraphs: The previous citation was an unverified local publisher record at content/modules/anthropic-claude-practice/claude-safety-and-trust-boundaries.json. During this review, it was replaced with official National Institute of Standards and Technology guidance and Anthropic's official Responsible Scaling Policy.

This change affects the module's source attribution and the support for its risk-management guidance. The correction also makes clear that the controls described here are application design practices, not claims about undocumented Claude features or internal safeguards. The learning level, trust-boundary method, and emphasis on independent authorization remain unchanged.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand basic prompts, model responses, and the idea that an application can pass information between components. It does not assume knowledge of security engineering, a particular programming language, or undocumented provider controls.

A trust boundary is a point where data or a requested action moves between parties or components that should not automatically trust one another. In an application using Claude, boundaries can exist between a user and the application, between retrieved material and a prompt, between Claude's response and application logic, and between the application and a person or system able to cause an external effect.

sections.title: Separate content from authority
paragraphs: Claude can produce text that looks like an instruction, approval, classification, or decision. The form of that text does not give it authority. Application logic should decide whether an action is permitted by consulting an independent source of authorization rather than treating the model's wording as permission.

For example, a response recommending that a record be changed can be useful as input to a decision. The response should not, by itself, establish that the requester is allowed to change the record. Authorization belongs outside the model response and should be evaluated at the boundary before the action occurs.
This distinction lets you use model output while limiting its power. The model supplies content or analysis. A separate control supplies permission.
sections.callout: A model response may recommend an action, but it should not be the sole source of authority for that action.

sections.title: Map the boundaries
paragraphs: Start by tracing information from its origin to its possible effect. Identify who supplied each input, whether external content can influence the prompt, what the model returns, and what could consume that return.

Mark a boundary whenever information enters from a party that is not already trusted for the intended decision. User text, retrieved documents, and model output should be evaluated according to how they will be used. Data that is acceptable for summarization may not be acceptable as authorization for an external action.

Then classify the possible consequence. A low-consequence response that a person merely reads may need fewer controls than a response used to disclose information, alter a record, or trigger another consequential action. The control should be chosen according to the consequence, not according to how confident or polished the response sounds.

sections.title: Place independent controls
paragraphs: At each consequential boundary, apply a control that does not depend only on the model agreeing that an action is safe. Examples of control types include checking the requester's authority, validating the structure and allowed range of data, limiting the actions available to the application, and requiring human review before a high-consequence action.

Independent controls provide defense in depth. If misleading input changes a model response, the next boundary can still reject an unauthorized or invalid action. The purpose is not to assume that every response is wrong. It is to prevent one response from becoming the only barrier between untrusted input and a consequential effect.

Model-level safety measures and application-level controls address different parts of the risk. A provider may apply safeguards to a model, while the application owner still determines what data the application accepts, what authority a user has, and which effects require additional approval.

sections.title: Apply the review method
paragraphs: For each path through the application, ask four questions. First, where did the information originate? Second, which component is being asked to trust it? Third, what consequence could follow if it is incorrect or adversarial? Fourth, which independent control stands between that information and the consequence?

A boundary is incomplete when the answer to the fourth question is only that Claude will decide whether its own output is safe. Improve that boundary by adding a separate authorization check, constrained action scope, validation step, or human decision suited to the consequence.

After this module, you can create a basic trust-boundary review that follows information from input to effect, separates recommendations from permission, and identifies where an independent control is needed.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a Claude response and authorization?
choices: A confident response automatically authorizes the action it recommends.
A response can inform a decision, but permission should come from an independent authorization control.
Authorization is unnecessary when the response contains a detailed explanation.
questions.explanation: The module separates content from authority. Claude may provide analysis or a recommendation, but an independent control should determine whether an action is permitted.

questions.prompt: When should an application designer mark a trust boundary?
choices: Whenever information moves from a party or component that is not already trusted for the intended decision.
Only after the application has produced an incorrect result.
Only where a person types the first prompt.
questions.explanation: The module defines a trust boundary as a point where data or a requested action moves between parties or components that should not automatically trust one another.

questions.prompt: Why should a consequential action have a control that does not rely only on the model's safety judgment?
choices: Because model responses can never be useful.
Because every model response must be rejected.
Because an independent control can still block an invalid or unauthorized action if misleading input affects the response.
questions.explanation: Independent authorization, validation, constrained action scope, or human review provides defense in depth between model output and a consequential effect.
